source.title: Harmfulness Propagation Dynamics: Layer-wise Trajectories of Adversarial Intent in Large Language Models
source.citation: Noor Islam S. Mohammad et al., 2026
source.authors: Noor Islam S. Mohammad; U. Bayazit

record.tranche_reason: Appendix N intervenes on learned harm directions during generation and measures refusal rates, testing a causal aspect of V1 with a different direction-estimation method and a single selected layer rather than the original all-layer difference-in-means intervention.
record.gate_note: The qualifying results are the generation-time refusal rates under harm-direction ablation in Appendix N, Table 17. The paper also cites prior work on refusal directions, but cited findings are not recorded as rows. Other reported results concern harm-prompt classification or moderator performance, not refusal-direction intervention; no addition-to-harmless-prompts or general-capability test is reported.
record.test_reason: Appendix N ablates a learned per-layer LDA harm direction (whitened harmful-minus-safe mean difference) at one layer. It measures generation-time refusal on 200 WildJailbreak prompts the models normally refuse, which bears on V1's ablation claim. The method differs from the original: LDA rather than raw difference-in-means, a single layer rather than all layers and positions, and ablation only, with no addition. The rest of the paper is prompt-harmfulness classification and does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors go further, saying the peak-layer harm direction is 'a causal locus at which the model's safety behavior is determined', with layer-specific effects. They do not claim full refusal removal, and they acknowledge limits from greedy 50-token decoding and judge inconsistency.
record.recipe_differences: Uses per-layer LDA harm directions rather than a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction; intervenes at one selected layer at a time rather than every layer and position; tests removal only, not addition to harmless prompts. The paper describes the generation experiment as consistent with prior refusal-direction work.
record.method_sensitivity: The ablation effect depends on layer: the peak-monotonicity layer produces a 33–35 percentage-point refusal-rate drop, versus 2.5–6.5 points at early or late layers in the table.

fits_no_version.finding: For harmful prompts, the last-token projection onto per-layer LDA harm directions rises monotonically with depth; benign prompts stay flat. Directions are stable across splits (cosine above 0.97), and LDA beats the class-mean difference by 0.5–0.8 F1 for classification.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The linear harmfulness representation of a prompt consolidates progressively across layers, and its trajectory shape is discriminative for harm classification.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper promises code and weights upon acceptance but gives no release URL)
record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
record.problems: The causal intervention uses only 200 prompts on which the models normally refuse, greedy decoding, and 50 generated tokens. No uncertainty estimate is reported for the refusal rates, and the outcome is judged by Llama-Guard-3, which the authors note may classify ambiguous completions inconsistently. The tested intervention is at a single layer at a time, not an all-layer ablation; no general-capability evaluation is included.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying refusal-direction intervention results are reported. Classification, benchmark, direction-stability, and benign-prompt true-negative results do not measure refusal-direction intervention or its predicted generation behavior.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; all-layer, all-position ablation with a raw difference-in-means direction; quantitative preservation of general capabilities (coherence is only asserted).
No test of attacks suppressing the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No causal comparison of multi-direction or cone accounts. Future subspace extensions are only mentioned.
No test separating the harm representation from the refusal decision, though the ablated direction is a harm-classification direction.
The Qwen3-8B-Thinking evaluation covers only prefill harm classification, with no ablation or refusal measurement.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label is downgraded to limits_scope: refusal is substantially reduced, not absent, and the setup differs from V1 (single layer, LDA direction). The study is a harm-moderation paper; the refusal ablation is a reviewer-requested appendix with no uncertainty estimates. The related-work section misattributes the refusal direction to Park et al. (2024).

versions.untested_parts: Uses per-layer LDA harm directions, not the stated difference-in-means direction; ablates only one layer at a time, not every layer and position; does not add the direction to harmless requests; does not quantitatively test preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration of released models.
No test that attacks suppress the direction and no training-against-ablation experiment.
No causal comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer test of refusal directions across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
No test of how refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
The paper evaluates its harmful-prompt moderator on a reasoning model, but does not test refusal-direction ablation or addition in that model.

relation.reason: Appendix N's own ablation results (Table 17) bear on whether removing a harm/refusal-related direction removes refusal. The rest of the paper is a moderation classifier and does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: Appendix N ablates a different direction (a per-layer LDA direction: whitened harmful-minus-safe mean, last token, trained on WildGuardMix) at one layer only. It measures generation-time refusal, so it is a different method on the same question V1 asks. It does not argue that V1 is wrong.

source_check.notes: Appendix N is a reviewer-response addition with no uncertainty, no random-direction control and no capability measure; the only comparison is across layers. The prose says early/late effects are 5–8 points but Table 17 gives 2.5–6.5. Baselines are 93–94.5% even though the prompts are described as ones the model 'would normally refuse'. Related work credits the refusal direction to 'Park et al. (2024)'; Appendix N cites Arditi et al. 2024.

statements.correction: Add N-O-early and N-O-late to the rows cited. For this study: single-layer zero-projection of a per-layer LDA harm direction, compared across layers rather than against all-layer ablation; 2 models; 200 WildJailbreak prompts; Llama-Guard-3 judge; greedy 50 tokens.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are correct: 94.5→61.0 (Llama-3.1-8B), 93.0→58.5 (OLMo2-7B), and early/late values 86.5–90.5. Minor bookkeeping issue: the statement cites rows N-L-peak, N-L-early, N-L-late and N-O-peak, but the 90.5% and 86.5% come from N-O-early and N-O-late. This study also has no all-layer comparison. Its contrast is peak layer vs. early (l=4) and late (l=30) layers, on two models with 200 prompts.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Peak-monotonicity-layer ablation in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and OLMo2-7B-Instruct on the tested WildJailbreak prompts
reader_labels.reason: Ablation lowers refusal but leaves most refusals in place (61.0% and 58.5% still refuse), contrary to the version's predicted removal of refusal; see N-L-peak and N-O-peak.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Early- and late-layer ablations in the two tested instruct models
reader_labels.reason: The effect is layer-dependent: early and late ablations reduce refusal much less than peak-layer ablation, so the causal result does not generalize uniformly across layers; see N-L-early, N-L-late, N-O-early and N-O-late.
